chapter.name: Exploring Some Geometric Themes
chapter.blurb: Two geometric themes: constructing self-similar fractals (Sierpinski Carpet, Sierpinski Gasket, Koch Snowflake) and visualising solids through their faces/edges/vertices, nets, shortest surface paths, projections (front/top/side views) and isometric drawing.

scope_in.item: Construct the Sierpinski Carpet and Sierpinski Gasket fractals by repeated removal of a central piece, and find the number of remaining pieces and holes at a given step using the recursive relations shown in the chapter
Construct the Koch Snowflake fractal by repeatedly replacing the middle third of every side with two new sides, and find the number of sides and the perimeter at a given step
Recognise fractal-like self-similar patterns in human-made art and architecture, such as the Kandariya Mahadev Temple, Nigerian Fulani wedding blankets, and M.C. Escher's 'Smaller and Smaller'
Identify faces, edges and vertices of solids, and name and count them for prisms and pyramids with an n-sided polygonal base, including recognising the regular tetrahedron

Identify and construct nets of a cube (including which of several candidate layouts are valid, and that a cube has 11 distinct nets), a cuboid with given dimensions, and a regular tetrahedron (2 distinct nets)

Identify and construct nets of a cylinder (two circles and a rectangle whose length equals the circumference) and a cone (a circle and a sector), and state as facts the number of nets of an octahedron (11) and a dodecahedron (43,380), and that a sphere has no flat net

Find the shortest path between two points on the surface of a cuboid by unfolding it into a net, trying different valid unfoldings, and using the Baudhayana (Pythagoras) theorem to compute straight-line distances on the net
Define the projection of a point and of an object onto a plane using a perpendicular foot, and relate this to the earlier idea of an object's profile from a viewpoint

Determine when a projected line's length equals its actual length (only when the line is parallel to the plane), and that projection preserves parallel lines, so a parallelogram's projection is always a parallelogram

Identify the front view, top view and side view of a solid or a combination of identical cubes, draw these views, and match a given solid to its three views (or vice versa), understanding that a projection does not uniquely determine the object

Define the isometric projection of a cube (balanced on a corner vertex) as a regular hexagon, and identify the three principal axes -- height, length and depth -- associated with the three directions of an isometric grid
Draw combinations of identical unit cubes on an isometric grid by counting units along the height, length and depth axes

scope_out.item: Computing surface area or volume of any solid named in this chapter (cuboid, cylinder, cone, prism, pyramid, etc.)
scope_out.reason: This chapter is entirely about visualising, representing, and unfolding solids -- no surface area or volume formula is introduced or used anywhere in it

scope_out.item: The fractal dimension formula (D = log N / log s) or any measure of a fractal's dimension
scope_out.reason: The chapter only asks students to count remaining pieces, holes, sides and perimeter at a given finite step using simple recursive multiplication; it never introduces the concept of fractal dimension or logarithms

scope_out.item: Infinite sums or limits of the perimeter/area sequences of the Koch Snowflake or Sierpinski fractals
scope_out.reason: All 'Figure it Out' questions ask for the value at the nth step (a finite step number), never for the limiting value as n approaches infinity

scope_out.item: Euler's formula (F + V - E = 2) named or applied explicitly
scope_out.reason: The chapter has students count faces, edges and vertices directly and by pattern for prisms and pyramids, but never names or states Euler's formula

scope_out.item: Trigonometric ratios or vector methods for computing projections
scope_out.reason: Projection is defined only informally via a perpendicular foot from a point to a plane; no sine, cosine, or vector-based calculation is used anywhere in the chapter

scope_out.item: The icosahedron, or any Platonic-solid classification beyond the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron and dodecahedron the chapter actually names
scope_out.reason: The chapter mentions only these four solids by name in its nets discussion; it never introduces the icosahedron or the general theory of the five Platonic solids

scope_out.item: A formal proof of why the isometric projection of a cube preserves equal edge lengths
scope_out.reason: The chapter poses this as a 'Math Talk' discussion prompt ('try to understand why') rather than providing or requiring a written proof

scope_out.item: Deriving or counting the number of nets of an octahedron (11) or a dodecahedron (43,380) from first principles
scope_out.reason: These counts are given to students as stated facts about which mathematicians have determined the totals; the chapter does not ask students to derive or verify them

scope_out.item: Surface-path shortest-distance problems on solids other than a cuboid, such as a cylinder or a cone
scope_out.reason: Every ant-and-laddu shortest-path example and exercise in the chapter uses a cuboid; cylinders and cones appear only in the separate nets discussion, not in the shortest-path problems

scope_out.item: The 'impossible triangle' (Figure it Out Q4 on p.101) as a testable exercise beyond simple recognition that it cannot be built from real cubes
scope_out.reason: The chapter poses it as an open visualisation discussion prompt without a definite numeric or provable answer, so it is not suitable for a graded question

concepts.name: Sierpinski Carpet and Sierpinski Gasket
concepts.description: Building these two fractals by repeatedly removing a central piece, and finding the number of remaining pieces and holes at a given step.
concepts.idea: Repeating one simple geometric rule on a shape, over and over at smaller and smaller scales, produces a fractal -- a shape that looks similar to itself at every scale.
concepts.rule: Sierpinski Carpet: start with a square (Step 0), divide into 9 equal smaller squares and remove the centre one (Step 1), then repeat the same rule on each of the 8 remaining squares. If R(n) is the number of remaining smallest squares at step n, R(n+1) = 8 R(n) and R(0)=1, so R(n) = 8^n; if H(n) is the number of holes, H(n+1) = H(n) + R(n). Sierpinski Gasket: start with an equilateral triangle (Step 0), join the midpoints of its sides to break it into 4 identical smaller triangles and remove the central (inverted) one (Step 1), then repeat on each of the 3 remaining triangles.
concepts.example: At Step 2 of the Sierpinski Carpet, each of the 8 squares from Step 1 is itself divided into 9 and has its centre removed, leaving 8x8=64 remaining squares.

questions.a: The claim is not consistent with the formula. concepts.name: Koch Snowflake and Fractals in Art
concepts.description: Building the Koch Snowflake by replacing the middle third of every side, finding its side count and perimeter at a given step, and recognising self-similar fractal patterns in real-world art and architecture.
concepts.idea: The same 'replace the middle third with a bump' rule, applied to every side again and again, turns a triangle into the ever more detailed Koch Snowflake, and the same self-similar repetition appears in human-made art and architecture.
concepts.rule: Starting from an equilateral triangle (3 sides), each step divides every side into 3 equal parts, raises an equilateral triangle outward on the middle part, and removes that middle part, replacing each side with 4 shorter segments. The number of sides at step n is S(n) = 3 x 4^n, and the perimeter is P(n) = 3 x (4/3)^n if the starting side length is 1 unit. Self-similar, fractal-like patterns also appear in human-made art and architecture, such as the Kandariya Mahadev Temple (Khajuraho), Nigerian Fulani wedding blankets, and M.C. Escher's print 'Smaller and Smaller'.
concepts.example: A Koch Snowflake starting with a triangle of perimeter 3 units has perimeter 3 x 4/3 = 4 units after Step 1.

questions.a: The reasoning is not sound. s: States the reasoning is not sound / area behaves differently from perimeter

s: Describes a clear division-and-raise rule for a new fractal on a square
States correctly whether the perimeter grows, shrinks, or stays the same under this rule

concepts.name: Solids: Faces, Edges, Vertices, and Nets of Cube, Cuboid and Tetrahedron
concepts.description: Naming and counting the faces, edges and vertices of prisms and pyramids, and identifying and constructing valid nets of a cube, a cuboid and a regular tetrahedron.
concepts.idea: A solid can be described by its faces (flat surfaces), edges (where two faces meet) and vertices (corner points), and many solids can be built by folding a flat 'net' -- a 2-D shape that folds up into the solid.
concepts.rule: A cuboid/cube has 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. A prism has two congruent polygon 'end' faces plus parallelogram side faces; an n-sided-base prism has (n+2) faces, 3n edges, 2n vertices. A pyramid has one polygon base and triangular side faces meeting at an apex; an n-sided-base pyramid has (n+1) faces, 2n edges, (n+1) vertices. A triangular pyramid with all faces equilateral triangles is a regular tetrahedron. A cube has 11 distinct nets (up to rotation/flip); a regular tetrahedron has only 2 distinct nets. Not every arrangement of the right number of squares (or triangles) is a valid net -- the pieces must fold up without gaps or overlaps.
concepts.example: A pentagonal prism has 5+2=7 faces, 3x5=15 edges, and 2x5=10 vertices.

concepts.name: Nets of Cylinder and Cone, and Shortest Paths on a Cuboid
concepts.description: Constructing nets of curved solids, and finding the shortest path between two points on a cuboid's surface by unfolding it and using the Baudhayana (Pythagoras) theorem.
concepts.idea: Curved solids like cylinders and cones can also be 'unfolded' into flat nets, and unfolding a solid's surface turns the problem of finding the shortest path between two points on the solid's surface into an easier problem of finding the shortest straight-line path on the flat net.
concepts.rule: A cylinder's net consists of 2 circles (top and bottom) and 1 rectangle (the curved side unrolled); the rectangle's length equals the circle's circumference (2 pi r) and its width equals the cylinder's height. A cone's net consists of 1 circle (the base) and a sector of a larger circle (the unrolled curved surface), whose radius equals the cone's slant length. A sphere has no flat net that wraps around it without wrinkles or gaps. On a cuboid, the shortest path between two points on its surface is found by unfolding the cuboid flat along the faces the path crosses and drawing the straight-line distance on the net; different unfoldings give different straight-line lengths, so multiple unfoldings must be tried, and right-triangle side lengths on the net are found using the Baudhayana theorem (Pythagoras theorem).
concepts.example: Unfolding two adjacent faces of a cuboid into one flat rectangle of size 24 cm by 32 cm turns a surface-path problem into finding the diagonal of that rectangle, which is sqrt(24^2+32^2) = 40 cm using the Baudhayana (Pythagoras) theorem.

concepts.name: Projections: Front, Top and Side Views
concepts.description: Defining the projection of a point and an object onto a plane, and identifying, drawing and matching the front, top and side views of solids and cube combinations.
concepts.idea: The view of a solid from one direction alone doesn't fully describe it, so engineers standardise on three mutually perpendicular projections -- front view, top view, and side view -- to represent a 3-D solid on a flat page.
concepts.rule: A point's projection on a plane is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from that point to the plane; the projection of an object is the set of projections of all its points. The length of a projected line segment is always less than or equal to its actual length, and equals it only when the segment is parallel to the plane it's being projected onto. Parallel lines project to parallel lines, so a parallelogram's projection is always a parallelogram. The front view is the projection onto the vertical plane in front of the object, the top view onto the horizontal plane below it, and the side view onto the side plane; a given projection does not uniquely determine the object.
concepts.example: A cylinder standing upright has a rectangular front view, a circular top view, and a rectangular side view (identical to the front view).

concepts.name: Isometric Projections and the Isometric Grid
concepts.description: Defining the isometric projection of a cube as a regular hexagon, and drawing combinations of unit cubes on an isometric grid along the height, length and depth axes.
concepts.idea: When a cube is oriented so all its edges project to equal lengths (balanced on a corner), its projection -- called an isometric projection -- is a regular hexagon, and tiling the plane with such hexagons gives an isometric grid on which 3-D combinations of cubes can be drawn with all unit lengths preserved along three principal directions.
concepts.rule: 'Isometric' means 'equal measure'. On an isometric grid, the three families of parallel edges correspond to the height, length and depth axes of the solid being drawn; a vertical line on the paper always represents the height axis, while the two slanted directions represent length and depth. Because projection preserves parallel lines and the isometric projection preserves equal unit lengths along all three axes, a solid built from unit cubes can be drawn accurately on the isometric grid by counting grid units along the appropriate axis for each edge.
concepts.example: A 1x1x1 cube is drawn on isometric paper as a hexagon outline with three visible faces (top, front-left, front-right), each drawn as a rhombus with all sides of equal length on the grid.
